iOS 27 Beta 5 contains code related to a new feature that allows Apple to verify the authenticity of iPhone photos.

The vast majority of iPhone users will never need this feature, which I'll explain in a moment, but this move is just the beginning...

What is Apple Reference Image?

AI-generated images and videos are advancing rapidly, reaching levels of realism and detail that can sometimes be indistinguishable from real photos. This fact is being exploited by scammers and those deliberately spreading misinformation.

An industry organization has been formed to address this situation, called the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA). It provides methods to identify authentic photos and allows viewers to understand how a photo has been modified, whether using AI tools or not.

More than 500 companies have joined the C2PA initiative, but Apple appears to be going its own way for now, launching the Apple Reference Image (ARI) feature. Anyone who takes a photo with an ARI-enabled iPhone can upload it to Apple's servers to verify its authenticity.

Why is this only a beginning?

Resources discovered in the latest beta indicate that the ARI feature will be off by default, since most iPhone users simply don't need it. It is primarily aimed at journalists and those involved in legal proceedings, who may need to provide independent evidence that their photos are authentic.

However, the initial applications of ARI may be limited, but as the use of AI image generation increases, such features will become increasingly common. For example, the EU recently announced a code of practice regarding transparency for AI-generated content, aimed at allowing people to easily distinguish whether content is fake. The code applies to both images and text (see below).

The initiative is currently voluntary, but several AI heavyweights have already positioned themselves in support. Anthropic says all future Claude models will include digital watermarks for text and images. Notably, the company will implement this globally rather than just in EU countries — which essentially means they expect such requirements to likely become mandatory worldwide in the near future.

How to verify text authenticity?

The most striking requirement in the EU plan is that AI companies must add digital watermarks to text outputs (not just images).

This can be done through invisible characters, like the one I just used to replace the space between "invisible" and "characters". This method survives copy-pasting, although it can be easily defeated using OCR. For example, there's a tool on my Mac that handles this as easily as taking a screenshot (I installed it because some companies like to post statements as images on social media, which is really annoying).

Some have suggested Anthropic may go further and use specific language patterns in Claude's output so that even text processed through OCR can be detected. I have a lot of thoughts on this, but they are beyond the scope of this article.

If such requirements ultimately become mandatory, Apple will need to apply them to tools like Siri AI rewriting.

What do you think about this trend? Feel free to share in the comments section.
